In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in vitro adventitious root initiation is a useful technique for the rapid and efficient production of microcuttings for subsequent transplant.
the in vitro adventitious root initiation process is a highly complex and dynamic phenomenon, and that in vitro adventitious rooting is not a simple, one-step procedure.
the anatomical and physiological properties of in vitro and of ex vitro adventitious root initiation are different and, as a result, the quality of the microcuttings is affected.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the in vitro rooting treatment was superior for root initiation but inferior for acclimatization.
in vitro adventitious root initiation is a very efficient process, but that ex vitro rooting and post-transplant root acclimatization are necessary for the production of a high-quality plant.

the anatomical, physiological, and morphological characteristics of in vitro- and ex vivo-rooted microcutting roots continue to influence the growth and quality of plants in later stages of micropropagation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the root initiation method can have a profound effect on the quality of microplants, and that the anatomical and morphologic differences between in vitro and ex vivo rooted microplants continue to influence their performance in later stages of plant production.
the in vitro environment can lead to the production of roots which are anatomically different from roots produced under ex vitro conditions.

the in vitro rooting process has a profound effect on the root system of the plant, and this effect continues to be manifested in later stages of plant development, even though the anatomical features of the root system have returned to a normal state by the time of transplant.
